newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: SIMEX conducting major review of energy futures.
newsitem.headline: SIMEX conducting major review of energy futures.

text.p: The Singapore International Monetary Exchange (SIMEX), battling illiquidity, is conducting a complete review of its energy future contracts, industry sources said on Wednesday.

"We are currently working with our energy contract committee and are in the process of conducting a complete review with the (energy) industry on its risk management needs via the use of the future contracts," a SIMEX official said.
The exchange planned to carry out a survey of the oil industry and speak individually to traders, another SIMEX official said.
The officials declined to be named.
One source said the exercise would help identify weaknesses in the currently listed Brent and high sulphur fuel oil contracts and to find ways of increasing the volume of trade.
SIMEX plans a meeting with the International Petroleum Exchange (IPE) in London in November to explore ways of boosting trade in the Brent crude contract.
A SIMEX official said the survey exercise would be completed later this year and would not be to be presented at the meeting.
The Brent contract, launched last year, trades in line with the Brent contract on the IPE. The two exchanges operate a mutual offset system.
The fuel oil contract was launched in February 1989 but trade ground to a halt early last year owing to illiquidity. Traders said the specification of the fuel oil was not in line with market needs.
Other SIMEX futures contracts have also failed to take off in the past few years.
SIMEX launched a Dubai contract in June 20, 1990, and delisted it on June 31, 1992. A gasoil contract launched in 1991 was delisted in June 1993.
The absence of highly liquid futures contracts in crude or products has puzzled many analysts.
Asia is the world's fastest growing consumer of energy, guzzling 17 million barrels of crude oil a day. By early next century it is expected to be the biggest refining centre in the world.
"Logically, we should have a successful oil futures exchange, looking at the growth rate at this region," said an oil trader.
SIMEX earlier this year made recommendations to the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) for changes to the fuel oil contract.
The proposed changes included lowering the sulphur content to 3.5 percent from 4.0 percent and narrowing the loading-date window for physical deliveries against the contract.
MAS has yet to grant approval for the changes.
